summary: Describes conventions for using the SHA3 family of one-way hash functions with the Cryptographic Message Syntax. SHA3 can serve as a message digest, as part of a signature or message authentication code, and as part of a key derivation function.

eli5.summary: A hash is a way to squeeze any message into a short fingerprint. This explains how to use the newer SHA3 fingerprint makers inside signed and secret messages.

questions: how to use sha3 in cms

subtitle: How to name and use the four SHA3 hash functions for signatures, MACs and key derivation in CMS messages.

tldr.problem: The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) needs agreed identifiers and encoding rules before it can use the SHA3 family of hash functions for digests, signatures, message authentication and key derivation.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC assigns object identifiers for SHA3-224, SHA3-256, SHA3-384 and SHA3-512 and for RSA and ECDSA signatures, HMAC and HKDF built on them. It also describes KMAC128, KMAC256, KDF2 and KDF3 use, and states exactly when the parameters field must be absent or NULL.
tldr.outcome: Implementations can use SHA3 in CMS in an interoperable way. The ASN.1 module in the appendix collects every identifier in one place.

today: RFC 9688 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2024. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: What This RFC Covers
sections.content:
The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS, RFC 5652) is used to digitally sign, digest, authenticate or encrypt arbitrary message contents. This RFC describes how to use the four one-way hash functions of the SHA3 family (SHA3-224, SHA3-256, SHA3-384 and SHA3-512) with CMS.

It also covers using those hash functions with the RSASSA PKCS#1 version 1.5 signature algorithm and with the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) in the CMS signed-data content type. The RFC says it should not be confused with RFC 8702, which does the same job for the SHAKE family of SHA3-based extensible output functions.

CMS values are generated with ASN.1 using the Basic Encoding Rules (BER) and the Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER).
sections.eli5: CMS is a kind of envelope for signed and secret messages. This RFC says how to label the envelope when the sender uses the SHA3 fingerprint makers.

sections.title: Message Digest Algorithms
sections.content:
One-way hash functions are also called message digest algorithms. Their identifiers appear in the SignedData digestAlgorithms field, the SignerInfo digestAlgorithm field, and the digestAlgorithm fields of DigestedData and AuthenticatedData. Digest values appear in the DigestedData digest field and in the Message Digest authenticated attribute, and they are also the input to signature algorithms.

SHA3-224, SHA3-256, SHA3-384 and SHA3-512 produce outputs of 224, 256, 384 and 512 bits. Each has an object identifier (OID) under the NIST hash algorithm arc, numbered 7, 8, 9 and 10.

When any of these four identifiers is used, the parameters field MUST be absent. The RFC stresses that this means absent, not NULL.
sections.eli5: There are four sizes of fingerprint, small to large. Each has its own name tag, and the name tag must not carry any extra notes.

sections.title: Signature Algorithms
sections.content:
Signature algorithm identifiers and signature values live in the SignerInfo signatureAlgorithm and signature fields, including those inside countersignature attributes. The RFC defines identifiers for RSASSA PKCS#1 v1.5 and for ECDSA, each paired with one of the four SHA3 functions.

For RSA, the identifiers are numbered 13 to 16 under the NIST signature arc. The parameters field MUST contain NULL for these and for rsaEncryption. The public key is encoded as an RSAPublicKey (modulus and public exponent) as in RFC 3279. The single value the algorithm produces is used directly as the signature value.

For ECDSA, the identifiers are numbered 9 to 12. Here the parameters field MUST be absent. Public key conventions follow RFC 5480, and the ECParameters in the signer's certificate apply to verification. ECDSA produces two values, r and s, which MUST be carried together as an ASN.1 ECDSA-Sig-Value sequence.
sections.eli5: A signature is like signing your name on a fingerprint. RSA gives one long scribble. ECDSA gives two numbers, so they are tied together in one package.

sections.title: Message Authentication with HMAC
sections.content:
A message authentication code lets someone who shares a secret key check that a message was not changed. The RFC covers HMAC (RFC 2104) with each SHA3 function. The algorithm identifier goes in the AuthenticatedData macAlgorithm field and the result in its mac field.

The four HMAC identifiers are numbered 13 to 16 under the NIST hash algorithm arc. As with the plain digests, the parameters field MUST be absent.
sections.eli5: An HMAC is a fingerprint that only people who know a secret password can make. If the fingerprint matches, nobody tampered with the message.

sections.title: Key Derivation Functions
sections.content:
A key derivation function (KDF) turns one secret into keying material. The CMS KEMRecipientInfo structure from RFC 9629 is one place that needs KDF algorithm identifiers. The RFC defines three groups.

  • HKDF with SHA3 (RFC 5869): four identifiers numbered 32 to 35 under the S/MIME algorithm arc, with the parameters field absent.
  • KMAC128-KDF and KMAC256-KDF: take a key K, a context X, an output length L in bits and an optional customization label S. The lengths of K and S MUST be less than 2^2040, and L must be at least 0 and less than 2^2040. The parameters field is absent when there is no label. If a label is given it MUST be present, encoded as an OCTET STRING.
  • KDF2 and KDF3 (from ANSI X9.44): the parameters carry a digest algorithm identifier naming the hash in use, which for SHA3 is one of the identifiers from the digest section.
sections.eli5: A key derivation function is like a juicer. You put in one secret fruit and get out as much key juice as you need. This section names the juicers that use SHA3.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC lists a few practical warnings. Implementations must protect the signer's private key, because its compromise permits masquerade. They must also protect the key-derivation key, because its compromise lets others derive the keying material.

When more than two parties share the same message-authentication key, data origin authentication is not assured, since any of them could have computed a valid MAC.

Random values must be generated well. Weak random number generators can leave keys, MAC keys and the per-message ECDSA k value easy to reproduce, and the RFC points to RFC 4086 for guidance. Finally, because algorithms weaken over time, implementations should be modular so new algorithms can be inserted.
sections.eli5: Keep your secret stamp locked away, use truly random numbers, and be ready to swap in better tools later.

sections.title: IANA and the ASN.1 Module
sections.content:
IANA assigned one OID for the ASN.1 module, id-mod-sha3-oids-2023, number 78 in the S/MIME module identifiers registry. It also assigned the four HKDF-with-SHA3 identifiers, numbers 32 to 35, in the S/MIME algorithms registry.

Appendix A holds the ASN.1 module that gathers all of the identifiers for digests, signatures, MACs and key derivation. It imports types from the modules in RFC 5912.
sections.eli5: IANA is the official keeper of the name list. It wrote the new SHA3 names into its book so nobody else uses them for something different.
